lead: Unit 3 is about context-free grammars: a few rewrite rules that generate nested structure such as aⁿbⁿ, balanced brackets and arithmetic expressions. You learn to derive strings, draw parse trees, remove ambiguity where possible, and rewrite any grammar into Chomsky or Greibach normal form. You also get the tools that prove a language is not context-free, the closure and decision properties, the CYK membership test, and the place of these grammars in the Chomsky hierarchy.
about: The unit builds one idea at a time. Chapter 3.1 gives the four-part definition of a grammar and five example languages. 3.2 turns the rewriting into derivations and parse trees, the same generation seen two ways. 3.3 uses two trees for one string to define ambiguity, and separates bad grammars from inherently ambiguous languages. 3.4 strips a grammar of epsilon rules, unit rules and useless symbols; 3.5 reshapes what is left into Chomsky and Greibach normal forms. 3.6 and 3.7 are the negative tools — the pumping lemma and closure properties — that prove a language is not context-free. 3.8 adds the CYK table, a dynamic-programming membership test that runs on a CNF grammar. 3.9 places all four grammar types in one nested hierarchy.

chapters.idea: A context-free grammar is a finite set of rewriting rules, and the language it generates is every terminal string reachable from the start symbol.
chapters.depth: Formal 4-tuple G = (V, T, P, S). V is the set of variables (nonterminals, written in capitals), T the terminals, P the productions, S the start symbol. Every production has the form A → α, where A is a single variable and α is any string of variables and terminals. Explain that 'context-free' means the left side is one variable, so a rule can be applied wherever A appears, with no test on neighbouring symbols. Cover the usual shorthand: the bar | for alternatives and grouping brackets. Give five example grammars with the language each generates: S → aSb | ε for {aⁿbⁿ}, balanced brackets, palindromes over {a, b}, arithmetic expressions, and a small grammar for if-else in C. Define ⇒ (one step) and ⇒* (many steps), and L(G) = {w ∈ T* : S ⇒* w}. Some syllabi call these type 2 grammars; the BNF used in compiler books is the same object with different punctuation.

figure.title: Anatomy of a grammar
figure.aria: The start symbol drives rules that use variables and terminals, and every string they can reach ends up in the language L(G).

chapters.example: G = ({S}, {a, b}, P, S) with P: S → aSb | ε. Derive aabb: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aabb. The only way to finish is to cancel the middle S, so every generated string has equal numbers of a and b, with all a before all b: L(G) = {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}. In order of length: ε, ab, aabb, aaabbb.
chapters.trap: Treating the grammar as the language. {aⁿbⁿ} is generated by both S → aSb | ε and S → ab | aSb. The bar | is shorthand for two productions, not a character of the language.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: alphabets, strings, languages, Kleene star.
chapters.leave: Derivations and trees in detail (3.2), normal forms (3.5), and the pushdown automaton that accepts these languages (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: A derivation is the step-by-step rewriting, a parse tree is the same rewriting drawn as a tree, and the tree is what a parser actually builds.
chapters.depth: Definitions: ⇒, ⇒*, sentential form, leftmost derivation (always expand the leftmost variable), rightmost derivation, yield or frontier of a tree, subtree, height. State the theorem: w ∈ L(G) exactly when some parse tree for G has yield w. State the matching theorem: every parse tree comes from exactly one leftmost derivation and exactly one rightmost derivation of that string. Work one string three ways — leftmost derivation, rightmost derivation, one tree — to show the tree does not record the order of rewriting, only the grouping. Note that the number of derivations of a string grows with the number of variables, which is why parsers store trees.

figure.aria: Parse tree for id + id × id; the multiplication sits deeper than the plus, so it is done first, and reading the leaves left to right gives the string.

chapters.example: Grammar: E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id. Leftmost derivation of id + id × id: E ⇒ E + T ⇒ T + T ⇒ F + T ⇒ id + T ⇒ id + T × F ⇒ id + F × F ⇒ id + id × F ⇒ id + id × id. That is 8 steps. The rightmost derivation expands F and T on the right first and takes 8 steps too. Both give the same tree, whose leaves read id, +, id, ×, id.
chapters.trap: Reading the tree from the top down as if that were the derivation order. The tree fixes grouping only. Also, an ambiguity check needs two different trees or two different leftmost derivations — two ordinary derivations that differ only in order prove nothing.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for grammar notation; Unit 1 for strings and concatenation.
chapters.leave: Ambiguity (3.3), grammar simplification (3.4), and parsing algorithms (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: A grammar is ambiguous when one string has two different parse trees, and a language is inherently ambiguous when every grammar for it is ambiguous.
chapters.depth: Define ambiguous grammar, ambiguous string, unambiguous grammar. Use E → E + E | E × E | ( E ) | id and draw both trees for id + id × id. Show that the layered grammar E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id encodes precedence and left associativity, and has exactly one tree per string. Some syllabi phrase the same topic as 'ambiguous CFG to unambiguous CFG'; give the recipe: add levels for precedence, choose left or right recursion for associativity, add a new start symbol if a rule is still needed at two places. Then inherent ambiguity: {aⁱbʲcᵏ | i = j or j = k} and {aⁿbⁿcᵐdᵐ} ∪ {aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ} are the standard examples; say the proofs need 3.6 and are not asked. Add one line: ambiguity of a given CFG is undecidable, proved in Unit 6.

figure.aria: Two parse trees for the same string: in one the plus is at the root, in the other the multiplication is, so the two groupings compute different values.

chapters.example: G: E → E + E | E × E | ( E ) | id. The string id + id × id has two trees. With root rule E → E + E the grouping is (id) + (id × id), value 1 + 2×3 = 7. With root rule E → E × E the grouping is (id + id) × (id), value (1+2)×3 = 9. Two trees, two meanings, so G is ambiguous. The layered grammar E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id has exactly one tree for the same string, and it is the 7 tree.
chapters.trap: Concluding a language is inherently ambiguous because your own grammar was ambiguous. Fix the grammar first; inherent ambiguity is a property of the language and needs a proof across all grammars.
chapters.leave: Normal forms (3.5); the pumping-lemma route to inherent ambiguity (3.6); undecidability of ambiguity (Unit 6).

chapters.idea: Removing epsilon productions, unit productions and useless symbols gives a smaller grammar for the same language.
chapters.depth: Define a nullable variable (one that derives ε), a unit production A → B with B a single variable, and a useful symbol, meaning both generating (it derives some terminal string) and reachable from S. Give the procedures in order. (1) Find nullable variables, then for each production add the versions obtained by deleting nullable variables from its right side, then drop A → ε; if ε ∈ L(G), keep the single rule S → ε and make sure S never appears on a right side. (2) For unit productions compute the unit pairs, then for each pair (A, B) with A ⇒* B add A → α for every non-unit rule B → α, and delete the unit rules. (3) Delete non-generating symbols, then unreachable symbols. Give the reason for the order: removing epsilon and unit rules can make symbols unused, so useless symbols go last. State the theorem that the final grammar generates the same language.

figure.title: Clean-up order
figure.aria: The clean-up pipeline: epsilon rules first, then unit rules, then useless symbols, and the language does not change.

chapters.example:
G: S → AB | a, A → aA | ε, B → bB | b, C → cC | c, D → aDb.
Step 1, epsilon: A is nullable, so add S → B (from S → AB) and A → a (from A → aA); delete A → ε. Now S → AB | B | a; A → aA | a; B → bB | b; C → cC | c; D → aDb.
Step 2, units: only S → B. Replace it by B's rules: S → bB | b.
Step 3, useless: D → aDb has no way to reach terminals, so D is non-generating and goes. C derives c, cc, … but no rule reaches C from S, so C goes.
Result: S → AB | a | bB | b; A → aA | a; B → bB | b. It generates the same language as G.
chapters.trap: Deleting useless symbols first. After epsilon and unit removal some variables become unreachable, so useless symbols must be removed last. Second trap: deleting the S → ε rule even though ε is in the language — keep it, with S absent from every right side.
chapters.leave: The CNF and GNF constructions (3.5); CYK, which expects a simplified grammar (3.8).

chapters.idea: A normal form fixes the shape of every production, so a proof or an algorithm has only two or three cases to check: CNF uses A → BC or A → a, GNF uses A → aα.
chapters.depth: Chomsky normal form: every production is A → BC with two variables, or A → a with one terminal; no unit rules; no ε rules except a possible S → ε with S absent from all right sides. Conversion pipeline: simplify (3.4), replace each terminal that sits next to variables by a new variable with a one-terminal rule, split right sides of length three or more into binary rules with fresh variables, then remove any unit rules created. Show the splitting rule in full: A → BCDE becomes A → BX, X → CDE, and then X → CY, Y → DE. Greibach normal form: every production is A → aα, where a is a terminal and α is a string of variables, possibly empty. Outline conversion: order the variables A₁ … Aₙ, substitute so that Aᵢ → Aⱼα only with j > i, remove left recursion, then expand the leading variables until each rule starts with a terminal. Note that GNF grammars have no ε rules and no unit rules, and say that both conversions can enlarge the grammar.

figure.aria: A right side of four symbols is broken into binary rules by two fresh variables, which is how CNF handles long productions.

chapters.example:
Convert G: S → aSb | ab to CNF. There are no ε rules and no unit rules. Introduce A → a and B → b, then replace terminals inside long rules: S → ASB | AB. Split S → ASB with a new variable X: S → A X and X → S B. CNF result: S → A X | A B, X → S B, A → a, B → b.
GNF example: S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. Substitute A's rules into S → AB: S → aAB | aB. Every rule now starts with a terminal, so the grammar is in GNF.
chapters.trap: Leaving a rule like A → aB in CNF — a terminal and a variable together is not allowed. Also A → BCD must become two binary rules, never stay with three variables. And remember the S → ε exception when ε is in the language.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 for the simplification steps that start every CNF conversion.
chapters.leave: CYK needs CNF (3.8); PDA to CFG conversions use the GNF idea (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: In any context-free language a long enough string repeats a variable on one path of its parse tree, so the two pieces around it can be pumped together.
chapters.depth: Statement: for every CFL L there is a pumping length p ≥ 1 such that every s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p can be written s = uvwxy with (1) |vwx| ≤ p, (2) |vx| ≥ 1, (3) uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for every i ≥ 0. Intuition: take a CNF grammar with b variables and p = 2^b; a parse tree for a string that long has a path with the same variable twice, once outer and once inner. The inner subtree gives w, the pieces around it give v and x, the rest gives u and y. Because v and x are pumped together, the lemma is weaker than the regular-language version, and it is only one-way: many non-CFLs also satisfy it, so failing to find a split proves nothing.

figure.aria: The same variable A appears twice on one path; the inner subtree gives w, the pieces around it give v and x, and the leaves read u v w x y.

chapters.example: Show L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} is not context-free. Assume it is, with pumping length p, and take s = aᵖbᵖcᵖ, length 3p ≥ p. Write s = uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p and |vx| ≥ 1. Since |vwx| ≤ p, the block vwx is shorter than one full block plus one more, so it cannot touch all three letters; some letter keeps count p in uv²wx²y. Pumping with i = 2 adds at least one symbol somewhere else, so the three counts can no longer be equal, and uv²wx²y ∉ L. Contradiction, so L is not context-free. The same argument with s = aᵖbᵖ shows {ww | w ∈ {a, b}*} is not context-free.
chapters.trap: Using |vx| ≤ p instead of |vwx| ≤ p. v and x may sit far apart inside vwx, and it is vwx that must be short. Also always check i = 0 or i = 2 explicitly, and remember the lemma cannot prove that a language is context-free.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for parse trees, 3.5 for CNF in the proof of the pumping length.
chapters.leave: Closure properties (3.7); the pumping lemma for regular languages is in Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal, homomorphism and intersection with a regular set, but not under intersection or complement.
chapters.depth: Give the grammar constructions: union with a new start symbol S → S₁ | S₂, concatenation with S → S₁S₂, star with S → SS | ε, reversal by reversing each right side, homomorphism by renaming terminals. For 'CFL ∩ regular' sketch the product of the pushdown automaton with the DFA, or build a grammar with paired variables — keep it to the idea and point to Unit 4. For non-closure use L1 = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and L2 = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ}; their intersection is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, not a CFL by 3.6. Derive failure of complement by De Morgan: intersection = complement of (complement L1 ∪ complement L2), so closure under complement plus closure under union would give closure under intersection. Then the decision properties that syllabi list with this topic: emptiness (does S generate any terminal string), finiteness (check for a usable variable that can reach itself), membership (CYK, 3.8), all decidable; and state that equivalence of two CFGs and ambiguity of a CFG are undecidable, with proofs left to Unit 6.

figure.aria: Two context-free languages whose overlap is aⁿbⁿcⁿ, and that language is not context-free, so the family is not closed under intersection.

chapters.example: L1 = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ | n, m ≥ 0} has grammar S1 → A C, A → aAb | ε, C → cC | ε. L2 = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ | n, m ≥ 0} has grammar S2 → A B, A → aA | ε, B → bBc | ε. Both are context-free. L1 ∩ L2 = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0}, which 3.6 shows is not context-free. So CFLs are not closed under intersection. For complement: if the complement of every CFL were a CFL, then L1 ∩ L2 = complement(complement L1 ∪ complement L2) would be a CFL by closure under union. It is not, so complement also fails.
chapters.trap: Reading 'CFL ∩ regular = CFL' as 'CFL ∩ CFL = CFL' — the regular side is what makes it work. Second, do not try to show complement failure by complementing {aⁿbⁿ}; that complement is a CFL. Use the De Morgan argument.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for grammar constructions; Unit 1 for regular languages and DFA; Unit 2 for closure of regular languages.
chapters.leave: The membership algorithm (3.8), the undecidability proofs (Unit 6), and PDA constructions (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: CYK fills a table of sets of variables for every substring, so membership of a string of length n costs about n³ rule checks once the grammar is in CNF.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this, so keep it short: the idea, the recurrence and one small table. Precondition: the grammar must be in CNF (3.5). Table V[i, j] holds the set of variables that derive the substring s[i..j]. Base case, j = i: A ∈ V[i, i] when A → s[i] is a rule. Step, for length ℓ = j − i + 1 from 2 to n: V[i, j] = union over k from i to j−1 of {A : A → BC, B ∈ V[i, k], C ∈ V[k+1, j]}. Accept when S ∈ V[1, n]. Time O(n³·|P|), space O(n²·|V|). Say that the table is filled by increasing length and that exams accept either the triangular layout or the n × n upper triangle.

figure.title: CYK table for aab, grammar S → AB, A → AA | a, B → b
figure.aria: The table for aab holds variables deriving one letter in the first row, pairs in the second, and the whole string in the last; the whole-string cell contains S.

chapters.example:
Grammar: S → A B, A → A A | a, B → b. Test w = aab.
Length 1: s[1..1] = a gives {A}; s[2..2] = a gives {A}; s[3..3] = b gives {B}.
Length 2: s[1..2] = aa, the only split is A with A, and A → AA gives {A}. s[2..3] = ab, split A with B, and S → AB gives {S}.
Length 3: for aab, split k = 1 gives {A} and {S} with no rule; split k = 2 gives {A} and {B}, and S → AB gives {S}. So V[1, 3] = {S}, S is in it, and aab ∈ L(G).
chapters.trap: Running the table on a grammar that is not in CNF — mixed rules like A → aB are simply skipped and the answer comes out wrong. Fill by increasing length, not row by row from the left, and read the answer from the cell for the whole string.

chapters.idea: Grammars are graded by how tightly the two sides of a rule are tied: type 0 unrestricted, type 1 context-sensitive, type 2 context-free, type 3 regular, each with its own machine.
chapters.depth: Give the four rule shapes. Type 0: α → β with α containing at least one variable and β anything, including ε. Type 1: αAβ → αγβ with γ ≠ ε, equivalently every rule is non-contracting, |left| ≤ |right|. Type 2: A → α with A a single variable. Type 3: right-linear, A → aB or A → a; left-linear grammars give the same class. Pair each type with its machine: Turing machine, linear bounded automaton, pushdown automaton, finite automaton; and with its language class: recursively enumerable, context-sensitive, context-free, regular. Show the inclusions are strict with one witness each: aⁿbⁿ is context-free but not regular (Unit 2), aⁿbⁿcⁿ is context-sensitive but not context-free (3.6), and the halting set is recursively enumerable but not recursive (Unit 6), hence not context-sensitive. Some syllabi call type 0 phrase-structure grammars; mention that the numbering runs from the most powerful to the weakest.

figure.aria: Four nested grammar classes, each with one witness language that belongs to it and not to the class inside it.

chapters.example:
Classify each language by the smallest grammar type that generates it.
(1) L = {aᵐbⁿ | m, n ≥ 0}: regular, type 3, grammar S → aS | B, B → bB | ε.
(2) L = {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}: context-free, type 2, not type 3 by the pumping lemma for regular languages.
(3) L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0}: context-sensitive, type 1; not type 2 by the pumping lemma in 3.6.
(4) L = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}: type 0 only, because it is not recursive (Unit 6).
chapters.trap: Mixing up the numbers — 0 is the most powerful and 3 the weakest. Also do not answer 'context-sensitive' for aⁿbⁿcⁿ without adding that it is not context-free, which is the part the exam is testing.
chapters.leave: Turing machines (Unit 5) and decidability, the halting problem and Rice's theorem (Unit 6).
